Nucleus—An organelle found in eukaryotic cells that houses the gene-containing
chromosomes of the cell and various nuclear proteins that communicate with the surrounding
cytosol via transportation through the nuclear membrane via pores. Clinically, karyotyping is
used to characterize the number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell.
Nucleolus—A prominent region in the nucleus of a cell that is responsible for the production
and assembly of ribosomes
Cytoplasm—The substance that is contained by the cell membrane and surrounds the nucleus
and is composed of water, salts, and proteins
Golgi apparatus (Golgi body)—An organelle that is responsible for the modification and
packaging of proteins and lipids that are released into membrane-bound vesicles
Lysosomes—Organelles responsible for the intracellular digestion of aged organelles, cellular
waste, and phagocytosed pathogens via acid hydrolases
Cell membrane—A double layer of phospholipids, or lipid bilayer, that encloses the cytosol,
nucleus, and other internal structures of a cell and acts as a protective barrier against the
external environment of the cell
Peroxisome—An organelle involved in lipid metabolism and the conversion of reactive oxygen
species
Mitochondria—Organelles with a double membrane that provide energy for the cell by
converting oxygen and nutrients into adenosine triphosphate
Ribosomes—Macromolecular machines that read the nucleotide sequence of messenger RNA
(mRNA) molecules and assemble the amino acids that correspond to specific triplet nucleotide
sequences (codons) in the mRNA to form proteins
Rough endoplasmic reticulum—An organelle covered in ribosomes, which are the site of
protein synthesis. This organelle is responsible for protein modifications.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum—An organelle lacking ribosomes that is responsible for the
synthesis of lipids and steroid hormones. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum of muscle cells
stores calcium and controls its release, thereby regulating muscle contraction and relaxation.
Cytoskeleton—An intracellular network of interlinking protein filaments, including
microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate fibers, that plays a critical role in maintaining
the shape and motility of cells and allows for the intracellular movement of organelles. The
cytoskeleton also is responsible for the contraction and relaxation of muscle fibers.

Eukaryotic cells are surrounded by a phospholipid bilayer and contain subcellular
structures that play critical roles in gene and protein expression, energy generation, and
metabolism (Figure 1). Various disorders are associated with the disruption of normal
functions of the organelles or subcellular structures. For example, lysosomal storage
disorders are a group of approximately 50 metabolic disorders that arise from defective
lysosomal function. Most commonly, these are the result of a deficient enzyme
necessary for the metabolism of lipids, glycoproteins, or mucopolysaccharides, resulting
in excess products being stored in the cells. Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher disease, and
Niemann-Pick disease are examples of lysosomal storage disorders. Conversely,
disruption in the structure of the cell membrane because of mutation in dystrophin
causes cell membrane fragility and permeability, resulting in Duchenne-type muscular
dystrophy. Finally, because the cytoskeleton provides structure, phagocytic action, and
motility, any defect in the arrangement of the actin filaments caused by stress or faulty
fiber production may result in loss of cell function and normal cell activity. Cytoskeletal
abnormalities may result in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies, defects in
phagocytosis and the motility of osteoclasts, some types of deafness, and other
disorders.

Extracellular Matrix
Extracellular matrix (ECM)—The noncellular portion of a tissue that provides structural support
for cells, affecting the development and biochemical and physiologic function of cells. The
bone ECM is maintained by osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes, whereas the cartilage
ECM is produced and maintained by chondrocytes.

Glycosaminoglycans—Structural polysaccharides composed of repeating molecules of a
disaccharide, including hyaluronic acid, dermatan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, heparin,
heparan sulfate, and keratan sulfate. Most glycosaminoglycans are covalently linked to a
protein core, resulting in molecules known as proteoglycans that are highly negatively charged
and provide the property of compressibility to cartilage. Hyaluronic acid, a nonsulfated
glycosaminoglycan, does not attach to proteins but becomes linked to various proteoglycans
to form giant molecules in synovial fluid that provide lubrication.

and contains tripeptide (Arg-Gly-Asp) sequences known as RGD domains, which are sites for
integrin binding, thereby playing a role in cell migration and differentiation

Elastin—Provides resilience to mechanical stress of many tissues, including tendon, elastic
cartilage, skin, and arteries
Laminin—An important component of the basal lamina. Laminin and type IV collagen form a
network for the basement membrane, an ECM structure that consists of a thin layer of
connective tissue. The basement membrane acts as a scaffold underlying the epithelial tissue
of the organs and supports the growth of epithelial cells.

Extracellular Matrix
The ECM of musculoskeletal tissues is predominantly composed of type I, type II, and/or
type III collagen; however, various other types of structural proteins also are important
in the proper structure and function of the ECM. Dysfunction of the ECM components
may directly contribute to musculoskeletal disease. In particular, genetic defects in
collagen may lead to several musculoskeletal diseases. Osteogenesis imperfecta is an
autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in type I collagen that result in bone
fragility and frequent fracture. Mild cases are caused by reduced levels of type I collagen,
whereas severe cases are caused by structural defects in collagen. Ehlers-Danlos
syndrome may be caused by several mutations in genes coding for various collagen
types, including type V collagen, and may lead to joint hypermobility, pain, and
dislocation; hyperextensible, weak skin with poor wound healing; and cardiovascular
abnormalities, including mitral valve prolapse and aortic aneurism. Alport syndrome is
caused by defective type IV collagen and is characterized by kidney disease and hearing
loss. In addition, deficient or defective fibronectin may lead to osteoporosis.
Intracellular Signaling
Cell response—Cells express specific genes in response to extracellular influences.
Signal transduction—Process by which an extracellular signal is transformed into an
intracellular message to elicit a specific response from a cell
Initiation of signal transduction—Binding of a specific ligand to a cell surface receptor initiates
signal transduction through various pathways, depending on the type of receptor.
Guanosine nucleotide-binding (G)-protein–coupled receptors—Binding of a ligand activates a
G protein, which functions as a molecular switch to hydrolyze guanosine triphosphate to

Ion channel receptors—Binding of a ligand alters the conformation of a specific ion channel.
The resultant movement of ions across the cell membrane activates a specific intracellular

Tyrosine kinase–linked receptors—Binding of a ligand activates cytosolic protein–tyrosine
kinase, an enzyme that transfers a phosphate group from adenosine triphosphate to

Receptors with intrinsic enzyme activity—Some receptors have intrinsic catalytic activity.
Examples include guanine cyclase activity, which converts guanosine triphosphate to cyclic

protein substrates.
Second messengers—Intracellular signaling molecules with a concentration controlled by the
binding of a specific ligand, or first messenger, to a particular type of receptor on the
membrane of a cell, including cyclic adenosine monophosphate, cyclic guanosine
monophosphate, diacylglycerol, inositol triphosphate, phosphoinositides, and calcium

Intracellular Signaling
Cell signaling is activated by various mechanisms, including ligand molecules binding to
cell surface receptors, mechanical forces, ECM interactions, contact with other cells, and
stimulation by hormones and cytokines. These pathways are critical for proper
development, cellular division, cellular differentiation, and homeostasis. For example,
bone morphogenetic proteins bind to serine/threonine kinase receptors, which activates
phosphorylation of the type I receptors that in turn phosphorylate SMADs.1 The
phosphorylated SMADs can bind to SMAD4 and then translocate to the nucleus to
activate target genes, including genes that promote osteoblast differentiation and are
important mediators of fracture repair (Resource 1). Orthopaedic tissues also are
subjected to various mechanical loads. Particularly, mechanical loading of cartilage may
activate anabolic pathways at physiologic mechanical loads to maintain tissue
homeostasis but activates degradative pathways and contributes to osteoarthritis
development under pathologic loading conditions2 (Resource 2). The interrogation of
cell signaling pathways is important in understanding normal and pathologic processes,

Genetics Basics
DNA-Related Terminology and Definitions
DNA—Double-stranded, helical polymer of covalently bound deoxyribonucleotides, consisting
of deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and one of the four bases—adenine, guanine, cytosine, or
thymine—that are paired through hydrogen bonds. The nucleotide sequence of DNA
determines the specific biologic information that is contained by each gene of a eukaryotic cell.
Central dogma of molecular biology—Genetic information is sequentially processed in a cell as
DNA→RNA→Protein.
Directionality—Single-stranded DNA is synthesized in a 5'-to-3' direction; it begins with the fifth
and passes sequentially to the third carbon of the cyclic sugar molecule that is a part of each
nucleotide in a strand of DNA.
Chromatin—Genetic material composed of DNA and proteins that is located within the nucleus
of the cell and condenses to form chromosomes
Chromosome—A nuclear structure that contains linear strands of DNA. Human chromosomes
contain 6 billion base pairs, which constitute approximately 50,000 to 100,000 individual
genes. Humans are diploid and have 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs.
Haploid: a cell containing one set of unpaired chromosomes
Diploid: a cell containing a paired set of chromosomes
Gene—DNA segment that contains all the information required for the synthesis of a protein,
including base sequences that participate in encoding a protein and noncoding sequences that
have other functions, such as determining when the gene is expressed
Genome—The full array of genes of an organism, encoding the structure of all its proteins and
other genetic information and, therefore, the fundamental structure and function of the
organism
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)—Circular DNA found in the mitochondria of cells. Mammalian
mtDNA are 16 kilobases long, contain very little noncoding DNA, and encode ribosomal RNA,
transfer RNA, and the proteins necessary for electron transport and the synthesis of
adenosine triphosphate within the mitochondria.

DNA polymerase—Enzyme that synthesizes new strands of DNA by linking individual
deoxyribonucleotides into polymers
Exon—Portion of a gene that encodes mRNA. Only 5% to 10% of genomic DNA in humans is
transcribed into mRNA.
Intron—Portion of a gene that does not encode mRNA
Gene promoter—Region of DNA that controls the initiation of gene transcription
Gene enhancer—Short region of a gene that, if bound by activating proteins, increases the
level of its transcription
Single nucleotide polymorphism—Alteration in the nucleotide sequence of a DNA molecule
caused by a change in one nucleotide
Epigenetics—Study of the manner in which environmental factors affect gene expression
without changing the base sequence of DNA
Genomics—Study of genomes and the functions of different genes

DNA-Related Terminology and Definitions
DNA encodes the genetic information that is passed down from one cell to another and
from generation to generation. Therefore, it is useful clinically to study genetic
inheritance, individual risk for various diseases, and a range of other applications.
Abnormalities in chromosome number, structure, or both are responsible for various
diseases, including Down syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, and various types of dwarfism.
Various orthopaedic disorders are caused by mutations in genes, including skeletal
dysplasias (Table 2), metabolic diseases of bone (Table 3), connective tissue disorders
(Table 4), musculoskeletal tumors (Table 5), and other musculoskeletal disorders (Table
6). In addition, mutations in mtDNA may cause neuromuscular disorders, thyroid
disease, cataracts, and diabetes mellitus. mtDNA originates from the maternal egg cells
of an individual; therefore, diseases inherited through mtDNA are passed exclusively
from mother to offspring. In addition, mutations throughout the noncoding regions of
DNA also may lead to pathology. Mutations in gene promotors are responsible for
several diseases, including Alzheimer disease, and mutations in gene enhancers are
responsible for other diseases, including Hirschsprung disease. Single nucleotide
polymorphisms are useful in diagnostics and investigation into the association of these
polymorphisms with various diseases and traits.

Nonsense mutation: resulting protein is interrupted by a newly introduced stop codon

Oncogenes promote unregulated growth through gain-of-function mutations that may
increase intracellular signaling.

Benign tumors do not spread to distant sites but may cause local destruction and are
managed via resection alone.

require aggressive local and systemic management and can cause death.

Basic Genetics
Gene therapy has been investigated as a means of correcting genetic disease via the
introduction of exogenous, normal genetic material into target germ cells, somatic cells,
or cancer cells. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-
CRISPR-associated proteins (Cas) system was discovered in bacteria as a means of
removing unwanted viral DNA from the bacterial genome. It has been investigated as a
gene editing tool with the advantages of low cost, simple manufacturing, and high
efficiency. Through CRISPR, DNA is modified by inducing cuts or breaks in defective
genes, using synthetic guide RNA to identify the DNA target and Cas endonuclease to
cleave the DNA. The gene is then removed completely or new DNA is added. Although
gene editing has become widely used in research, gene editing for human disease
remains experimental; however, clinical trials currently are underway to use CRISPR-
Cas9 gene editing to manage cancer, sickle cell disease, and blindness.3,4
Several genetic mutations lead to malignancies of the musculoskeletal system (Table 5).
Osteosarcoma is associated with the HST1 oncogene, which results in overexpression of
fibroblast growth factor. Fibrous dysplasia is associated with gain-of-function mutations
in GNAS1, resulting in constitutively active Gs protein. GNAS1 mutations occurring early in
embryogenesis result in McCune-Albright syndrome, marked by café-au-lait macules,
precocious puberty, and fibrous dysplasia. Contrarily, the retinoblastoma protein is a cell
cycle inhibitor, and loss of retinoblastoma protein may lead to osteosarcoma and other
sarcomas. TP53 is a tumor suppressor gene that regulates apoptosis, DNA repair, and
cellular division. It is commonly mutated in patients with cancer. Li-Fraumeni syndrome
is an inherited cancer syndrome resulting from a germline TP53 mutation, resulting in
multiple malignancies at an early age, including soft-tissue sarcomas and
osteosarcomas. Ewing sarcoma is a malignant, primary bone tumor resulting from
translocation and fusion of EWS on chromosome 22 to FLI on chromosome 11.

Innate and adaptive immunity—The body’s defense against pathogens and foreign substances
is mediated by innate immunity and adaptive immunity.
Intrinsic, or innate, immunity is the body’s early defense against foreign substances and
pathogens, with a rapid, but nonspecific, response to infection and damage. Intrinsic
immunity includes physical barriers, such as the epidermis, dermis, and mucosa; cellular
barriers, such as phagocytic cells and natural killer cells; and chemical barriers, such as
antimicrobial substances, blood proteins (complement system), and cytokines.
In adaptive immunity, exposure to a specific antigen initiates a process that prompts the
development of a group of immune cells that recognize that antigen and can rapidly respond
if it enters the body again. Successive exposure to the antigen increases the magnitude of
the immune reaction. Adaptive immunity includes two types of responses, known as humoral
and cell-mediated immune responses.
Humoral immunity—Mediated by antibodies, produced by B lymphocytes, that are directed
against specific antigens belonging to a foreign substance or pathogen, such as a virus or
infectious bacterium
Cell-mediated immunity—Mediated by T lymphocytes (T cells), which can activate
macrophages to kill phagocytosed antigens or can destroy infected cells directly
Immune mediators and regulation of bone mass
Cytokines, including tumor necrosis-a, IL-1, and IL-6, are low-molecular-weight, soluble
proteins that are produced by immune cells and facilitate and regulate the immune
response. Cytokines can induce immune cells to destroy foreign and pathogenic material;
however, overproduction of cytokines may cause destruction of normal tissue.
Cytokine storm, which can be precipitated by insults such as bacterial infection or
pancreatitis, is a systemic condition that may result in shock, end-organ damage, and death.
Inflammatory bone destruction or osteolysis occurs clinically in rheumatoid arthritis, chronic
inflammatory disease, periodontitis, and wear particle–induced osteolysis.
Anabolic factors, such as transforming growth factor-beta and bone morphogenetic proteins,
may stimulate the precursor cells of osteoblasts to differentiate into osteoblasts.

Several naturally derived materials currently are used in clinical practice. Small intestinal
submucosa has been used in soft-tissue repair, including anterior cruciate ligament,
meniscus, and rotator cuff in animal models.5-7 Membranes composed of porcine type
I/type III collagen were initially used to cover defects during autologous chondrocyte
implantation.8,9 These membranes currently are used as a delivery vehicle for
chondrocytes in matrix-assisted autologous chondrocyte implantation.10,11 More
recently, tissue-specific ECM biomaterials have been generated by decellularization of
native tissues that can be processed and used for tissue repair and regeneration.12-15
One example of a synthetic material is polyethylene glycol (PEG). PEG is a fairly inert,
nondegradable polymer that can covalently cross-link to form a polymeric network.
Several design modifications have expanded the versatility of PEG, including the
generation of complex multi-arm formulations that can nucleate cross-linking. Because
of the lack of biologic motifs, cell adhesion to PEG is poor. Therefore, to increase cell
adhesion, PEG has been modified to include ECM-mimicking peptides. In addition,
degradable cross-links have been engineered into PEG to enable cell-mediated
remodeling. Biodegradable polyesters, such as polylactic acid, polyglycolic acid, and
copolymers of the two, are other commonly used synthetics. In aqueous environments,
these polymers undergo hydrolytic degradation, and the degradation rate is modulated
by the polymer molecular weight and composition. Polylactic acid sutures and suture
anchors are popular in bioabsorbable orthopaedic implants. In addition, this polymer
and other polyesters currently are being used in scaffolds for regenerative medicine.

Rapid advances in 3D printing and rapid prototyping have allowed for the generation of
anatomic, 3D tissue-engineered constructs over the past several years.23,24 MRI,
microcomputed tomography, and in silico modeling generate information through
computer-assisted drawing programs to render 3D shapes via rapid prototyping. These
techniques allow for control of pore size and distribution and the production of scaffolds
in desired shapes with components that may promote cellular differentiation and tissue
formation. Image-guided tissue engineering facilitates the production of patient-specific
scaffolds that are size matched and well suited for orthopaedic applications. Using these
techniques, injection molding with cell-seeded materials has shown promise to generate
anatomic facial,25 meniscal,24,26 and articular cartilage implants.27 More recently, 3D
printing of porous scaffold materials has been used to control scaffold geometry and
pore sizes and spacing. These methodologies have been used to generate anatomic
replacements for the rabbit humeral head28 and to produce living, 3D tissue-engineered
cartilage constructs.12,29,30 These advances, in combination with the ability to culture
patient-derived stem cells, lay the groundwork for moving these functional tissue-
engineered scaffolds toward clinical use in the future.
